text: Nine minutes, and the eye on screen is usually looking back. Scott Bartlett keeps three subjects — an eye, a face, a body — and declines to hold any of them still, running them through fracture, doubling and color that turns over faster than it can be named. The soundtrack never settles either. What comes out stays stubbornly human: a face split into symmetry is still a face, and the shapes it throws off invite reading the way inkblots do. Celtic knots slide one into the next. Near the end a tree appears, and birds, white first and then red and blue, as though the world outside the apparatus had been remembered for a second. It is in the National Film Registry and still mostly unwatched. The frantic pitch is not a phase the film passes through; it is the condition of the whole thing, and it does not let up.

The zoo closes for the night and two people stay inside it. Zani has lived there all his life, easier with the animals than with anyone who buys a ticket; Eve is an orphan under school discipline strict enough to be worth escaping; and the moment they decide to be together, the grounds stop being a refuge and become a place being searched. Rowland V. Lee's picture runs a little over ninety minutes on a strange proposition: that the boy raised among cages is the least caged person in it, and that keepers with lanterns are the danger, not whatever is behind the bars. Romance built out of straw, locked gates and animal noise was not the usual American arrangement in 1933. The National Board of Review put it in its ten best, and the odd texture is the likeliest reason.

The family fortune is gone, and the joke is that nobody in the house knows how a job works. Nellie Rimplegar mishandled what the crash had not already taken; her sons treat wage labour as an exotic custom practised elsewhere; and Elizabeth, the one Rimplegar with a working grip on the calendar, becomes the person everything lands on, including a family doctor with intentions and a writer confident about matters he has not looked into. Elliott Nugent brings it in at seventy-eight minutes, roughly the right length for a comedy whose engine is a household being slowly introduced to consequence. It ran in the National Board of Review's ten best for 1933. The Depression is not the backdrop here; it is the thing at the door, and the laughs come from watching lunatics answer it.

The villain is called the Fuzz-Faced Phantom, and the man sent to catch him is Charley MacNeesha of Scotland Yard, travelling with an assistant named MacGregor. Nineteen minutes, made in 1928, and the paperwork on it is confused for good reason: haunted-house mystery, slapstick and animation share the same reel. Disruptions at the Frisbie house in New York are enough to bring detectives across an ocean, which is already the shape of the joke — enormous machinery brought to bear on a problem nobody can quite see. The straight face is what makes it work. A case is opened, a phantom is named, procedure is followed. Its place in the National Film Registry looks eccentric until the thing is actually running, at which point the mixture of horror décor and cartoon logic starts to explain itself.

A son sets out to find the man who should have stood in his father's place. The father was executed for a crime someone else committed, and what follows is less detection than a demand: that a stranger say out loud, to a witness, what was actually done. Seventy-seven minutes, 1936, and the Academy Award the film took for production design indicates where the effort went — into constructed space, a world assembled rather than borrowed from a street. Romance enters that frame and has to live inside it. Alfred Santell treats the dead man not as a character but as an unpaid bill, carried around by a young man who cannot settle it himself and cannot put it down either, and the picture is clear-eyed about the odds on a confession ever arriving from the people who owe one.

The claim, delivered in thirteen minutes and with a straight face, is that a tidy house survives an atomic blast better than an untidy one. Litter, peeling paint, a cluttered porch: in 1954 these could be presented as an invitation to the flash, and housekeeping as a branch of national defense. The logic is neither quite a lie nor quite an argument. It takes something real about fire and stretches it until it reaches the broom closet, where an ordinary citizen has some authority. That transfer is what makes the thirteen minutes worth spending now: a fear too large to hold gets handed back as a chore, and the handing back is done in the calm voice of instruction. The National Film Registry keeps it as a document of the period, though nothing in its tone concedes that it is one.

Yun Dong-ju wrote poems, and the record his film works from is a detention. Lee Joon-ik's 2015 biography comes at the life through the charge sheet — involvement in the Korean independence movement, custody under the Japanese, the treatment that followed — and that framing decides what the past is allowed to be. Not a career. A set of things a young man has to account for while somebody keeps a record of his answers. One hundred and eleven minutes, and the film is more interested in what it costs to say a sentence than in incident. It belongs to the Korean Film Archive's hundred, where the poems are assumed to be known already; the film takes that as permission to stay with the person, the friendships, the ordinary ambition to be published, rather than the reputation.

Ten minutes to noon, an inheritance that expires at twelve, and the bride is nowhere to be found. Alice Guy-Blaché's fourteen-minute comedy from 1913 runs on that clock and on nothing else, which is a sturdier design than it sounds: a deadline converts every street, doorway and passerby into either an obstacle or a shortcut, and the audience does arithmetic the whole way through. The groom's improvisations get less dignified as the minutes go, since a marriage attached to a will makes no requirement that anyone be enthusiastic, and the short never pretends otherwise. The National Film Registry keeps it, which suits a film built out of timing rather than sentiment — fourteen minutes that behave like a countdown, with a legal document doing the work a villain usually does.

Everything in this 1929 short is arranged to get Bessie Smith in front of a microphone. Dudley Murphy hands her a situation rather than a plot: her lover Jimmy, a gambler, has taken up with someone younger and prettier, and when he goes she sings, with a chorus and dancers filling the room behind her. Sixteen minutes. In 1929 recorded sound was new enough that a performance like this had to be treated almost as an event, and the film is organized to serve it — grievance first, then the number that turns grievance into shape. The all-Black cast in an American studio short of that year is part of why it is worth locating; so is the plainness of the setup, which asks nothing of the singer except that she be the woman the song is about. Its place in the National Film Registry rests on those minutes.

A film crew happens to be shooting on the same street where the theft occurs. That coincidence is the whole idea of this 1913 short: a messenger boy is accused of taking twenty thousand dollars in bonds, his accuser is convincing, the police are satisfied, and meanwhile a camera has been running with no stake in anybody's version of events. Fifteen minutes is time enough to plant the accusation and let it set. What makes it odd is the self-consciousness — a movie proposing, in 1913, that movies see things, and that a length of exposed celluloid might weigh more than a grown man's word in front of an officer. Lawrence Marston keeps the mechanics plain and the trust badly placed. The reel has no interest to protect. Everything then depends on somebody thinking to look at it.

A mountain fire pushes a wolf pack down into the desert, and the animal at the head of it is the one the film cares about. Lobo, played by Rin Tin Tin, is half wolf by pedigree and the protagonist by construction: hurt after drawing a posse away from the pack, he is taken in by a prospector, Dave Weston, and the friendship that follows has to be built without a line of dialogue. Around them 1925 conducts its business — a borax find, a rancher's daughter, a chemist called Borax Horton who would rather the claim were his. Seventy-four minutes, and the plot stays transparent by necessity, since a dog cannot state a motive and intertitles can only do so much. What is left is behaviour, watched closely: a Western in which the most legible performance has four legs.

Four episodes, four ways of shooting, and the same faces turning up across all of them. Ryoo Seung-wan's 2000 film takes male aggression as its subject and refuses to settle on one distance from it — violence as a group habit in one segment, as a private disposition in the next, the two set against each other by nothing more than proximity. Because characters cross between the parts, cause and effect come apart and are rejoined: what arrives as an incident returns later as a condition. Ninety-five minutes of crime picture in which the fights are staged to be understood rather than admired. It sits in the Korean Film Archive's hundred, and the anthology shape is not a stunt: it is the only arrangement that shows the same behaviour reading as character from one angle and as climate from another.

Tennessee, early in the century, and a household arranges its entire day around one man's coming and going. Alex Segal's film concerns the hours and weeks after an accident: who speaks, who cannot, and what is said to a boy old enough to ask questions and too young to be answered straight. The widow and the child are the whole scale of it. The National Board of Review counted it among the ten best of 1963, and the reason is conduct rather than incident — how a house reorganizes itself, how people raised not to discuss feeling still manage to convey a great deal, how relatives fill a silence they cannot mend. Ninety-seven minutes, much of it people sitting in rooms doing the ordinary tasks of a family whose arrangement no longer holds.
